title: connmark oscillation oncall diary — on‑prem firewall impact to control‑plane reachability
content:
Summary:

This is a working oncall diary for an incident on 2027-02-07 where a subset of on‑prem customer firewall appliances intermittently blocked control‑plane connections to Redwood Private control-plane endpoints. Symptoms presented as short (10–90s) windows where control-plane API calls returned TCP RSTs or 503s for management traffic routed via the customer's VPC edge. The outage surface was limited to managed control-plane IPs (10.200.5.0/24) — application traffic was largely unaffected.

High level hypothesis (current):
- A connmark oscillation was triggered by a sequence of NAT/marking changes during an internal policy sync on customer firewalls.
- Marks applied by userland firewall process were being cleared and then reapplied with different semantics across fast path vs slow path, causing subsequent netfilter rules to misclassify established control-plane connections and drop packets.
- The effect was amplified when nf_conntrack entry churn hit a threshold and conntrack started dropping entries; transient reclassification then left some connections effectively blackholed.

Detection / Monitoring timeline (UTC):
- 2027-02-07 02:13:21 — first alert: control-plane API error rate from region eu-west-1 rose above threshold (5m error rate spike to 8%). Alert routed to #sre-oncall.
- 02:14–02:18 — multiple customers behind on‑prem firewalls reported intermittent failures in the same window. Network team correlated by src subnet to particular customer edge cluster c-edge-7.
- 02:19 — oncall ran initial health checks: ping/tcp to control-plane IPs from a staging host behind same edge showed resets.
- 02:22 — kernel logs on customer edge showed: "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping" and frequent conntrack UDP/TCP timeouts.
- 02:24 — conntrack entries spiked (conntrack -L | wc -l: 214k) and nf_conntrack_max = 262144.
- 02:26 — iptables-save diff vs baseline showed new MARK/CONNMARK rules injected by customer firewall userland (policy sync).
- 02:30 — temporary mitigation (see below) implemented; errors subsided within 45s.

Investigative data collected:
- Kernel messages: journalctl -k from c-edge-7 showing nf_conntrack table warnings and netfilter mark restore messages.
- conntrack summary: conntrack -S reported heavy INSERT and DELETE churn; peak insert rate ~3.2k/s.
- iptables ruleset snapshots before/after (iptables-save). Notable new chains: FW-SYNC-POST, which calls MARK/CONNMARK save/restore.
- tcpdump capture on mgmt interface capturing RST patterns and mismatched seq resets during windows.
- ipvs/nftables logs where available; some edges were running nftables compatibility layer which rewrites connmark ops.

Immediate mitigations performed oncall (chronological):
1) Increase nf_conntrack_max temporarily on affected appliance: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288 (reduces immediate drop rate).
2) Insert emergency allow rule at top of filter table for control-plane management CIDR to bypass connmark-dependent chains: iptables -I INPUT 1 -s 10.200.5.0/24 -j ACCEPT (persisted as emergency entry in /etc/iptables/emergency).
3) Disable userland policy sync daemon (fw-sync) on the customer appliance in coordination with customer SRE lead to prevent further mark churn while we validated.
4) Re-run conntrack garbage collection: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait (tweaks to accelerate cleanup) and manual deletions for stale entries for 10.200.5.0/24 using conntrack -D.
Outcome: errors dropped back to baseline within ~45s of rule insertion and disabling fw-sync.

Root cause analysis (working):
- Trigger: a policy sync job on the appliance reloaded a set of firewall rules using a pattern that performs CONNMARK save/restore across a path that also includes SNAT. When the path included SNAT+connmark restore, some packets were processed in the slow path and marks were zeroed or changed unexpectedly.
- Race: concurrent connection churn + mark rewrite created short-lived entries where established flows were reclassified as NEW with no matching conntrack tuple — upstream control-plane then saw resets.
- Amplification: nf_conntrack table pressure (already high because of a bursty SCP/backup job) meant netfilter started evicting conntrack entries; when an entry was evicted mid‑reclassification, subsequent packets couldn't be matched and were dropped by later policy chains that depend on CONNMARK for explicit allow.
- Compatibility gap: on some appliances the firewall userland uses nftables shim that translates CONNMARK ops differently; mixing iptables-conv and nftables produced inconsistent behavior.

Commands & checks used during triage (copied for runbook):
- journalctl -u firewall-sync -f --no-pager\- grep -i nf_conntrack /var/log/kern.log\- conntrack -L | wc -l\- conntrack -S\- iptables-save > /tmp/rules.before && iptables -L -v -n\- tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.200.5.10 and port 443 -w /tmp/mgmt-cap.pcap\- sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max && sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288

Short-term runbook entries (DRAFT) to add to SRE playbooks:
- Detection: add alert for net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count / nf_conntrack_max > 80% (5m) and a combined rule for kernel messages containing "nf_conntrack: table full".
- Emergency bypass: documented command to insert top-level accept for control-plane CIDRs and persist emergency entry. Include automated script that can be run by oncall to insert the rule across appliance fleet via ssh or orchestration (with appropriate RBAC).
- Safe increase: guidance to increment nf_conntrack_max by +50% for appliances experiencing spikes, with instructions to revert and capacity cost notes.
- Policy sync: instruct customers and solutions engineering to prefer conntrack-neutral rule updates where possible; avoid sequences that remove/reapply connmark rules en masse.
- Compatibility test: add preflight test for fw-sync that validates conntrack neutrality (simulate short-lived flows + save/restore) in staging before rollout to prod.

Medium/long term engineering actions (owners assigned):
- Engineering (network infra): modify control-plane detection to prefer an explicit management fastpath that does not depend on CONNMARK semantics. (Owner: Arjun)
- Platform: provide a managed emergency-allow mechanism from control plane that can be toggled per-customer for reachability incidents (owner: Elena).
- Research: audit nftables compatibility shim on appliances and produce a doc with recommended CONNMARK/SNAT ordering to avoid mark clobbering (owner: Jon).
- Ops: add a periodic drain test that simulates conntrack churn scenarios and validates control-plane reachability.

Post-incident testing plan:
- Simulate a policy sync that performs CONNMARK save/restore + SNAT on a staging appliance while generating 10k short-lived connections to mimic backup/agent churn. Verify no control-plane connections are classified as NEW and dropped.
- Replay recorded tcpdump pcap against packet injection to confirm behavior.
- Run automation to elevate conntrack counts to 90% to confirm alerts and emergency bypass script correctness.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Was there any kernel backport on a subset of appliances that changes conntrack restore semantics? Need to cross-check package versions across fleet.
- Did the customer's recent config change introduce a new helper/conntrack module (FTP helper, etc.) that increased entry size and churn?
- Could an alternative approach using BPF-based marks avoid this class of bug? Worth a spike.

Action items (short list):
- SRE: publish this diary to Confluence and link SRE-1428 (Maya) — due 2027-02-09.
- Network infra: audit appliance kernel + netfilter versions for fleet variance and mark anomalies (Arjun) — due 2027-02-14.
- Platform: implement emergency allow orchestration prototype (Elena) — due 2027-02-21.
- Solutions: update customer-facing guidance and preflight checks for fw-sync before customer rollouts (Jon) — due 2027-02-18.

Notes to reviewer:
- This doc is intentionally written as an oncall diary + nascent runbook. Please add missing commands you used during triage, and flag any steps that are too invasive for self-serve emergency execution.
- If you have snapshots of iptables-save from the window, attach to SRE-1428.

Appendix: emergency commands (copy/paste with caution)
- Insert allow for control-plane CIDR:
  iptables -I INPUT 1 -s 10.200.5.0/24 -j ACCEPT
- Increase conntrack cap temporarily:
  sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=524288
- View conntrack counts:
  conntrack -S
- Delete stale conntrack entries for mgmt subnet (use with care):
  conntrack -D -s 10.200.5.0/24

End of diary.

(Last updated 2027-02-09 by Maya Chen)
